name: @cloudsforge/settlement
description: The outbound chain service. Treasuries, sweeps, outbound transaction building, signing requests, broadcast, confirmation tracking and stuck adjudication. One in-flight outbound transaction per chain per network, by construction.

scripts._test: --test-concurrency=1 is required, not a preference: every database test file truncates this service's tables between cases, and node:test runs FILES in parallel by default. A TRUNCATE takes an AccessExclusiveLock, so one file's reset deadlocks against another file's inserts (40P01). Cases within a file already run in order.

_localDependencies: Every sibling takes 'link:', not 'file:'. A 'file:' path PACKS the dependency, and each of
these packages declares files: ['dist'] with a publishConfig that points main/types at dist/.
Packing therefore installs a package whose exports resolve to a dist/ that has not been built,
while its 'main' in the working tree still says src/index.ts. 'link:' symlinks the checkout in
place, so the working-tree manifest is the one that is read and the package keeps using its own
already-installed node_modules — which is also what a 'workspace:^' transitive needs.
@cloudsforge/contracts-chain is EXACT-PINNED, never caret-ranged. This service and custody must
agree byte-for-byte about a chain id, because a skew there is not a 500: it is a signature bound
to the wrong network, and the transaction is broadcastable on the chain it was not meant for.
There is no EVM chain library here — no ethers. For EVM this service builds ONE transaction
shape (a legacy value transfer) and hands it to custody as a JSON object; custody is the
only place a private key exists and therefore the only place a serialiser is needed. What is
left is keccak256, for EIP-55 and for the transaction id, and that is sixty lines of permutation
rather than a dependency on the one path where a wrong answer sends money to a stranger.
bitcoinjs-lib IS here, and the paragraph above is exactly why it has to be. Its reasoning
depends on custody taking a JSON object, and that premise is false for Bitcoin: custody's
signBitcoin takes a base64 PSBT, because a segwit signature commits to the VALUE of each input
and only a PSBT carries it. Something on this side must encode BIP-174. The choice is then
between hand-rolling an encoder and using the library custody DECODES with, and it is the
second — a builder and a signer with two independent implementations of one binary format is
the precise shape of a bug that pays a stranger. Same package, same major version as custody.
@solana/web3.js is here for the identical reason and it is the stronger case: signSolana takes
a base64 WIRE TRANSACTION, so this side has to encode a compact-u16 account table, a header, a
blockhash and an instruction with account indices. Same package, same major version as custody
— so the bytes this repository produces are parsed by the parser they were produced for.
bs58 is the one place that argument is NOT satisfied, and it is deliberate. A Solana
transaction is identified by its first signature, base58-encoded — 64 bytes, which PublicKey
cannot encode — and @solana/web3.js does not re-export its own bs58. So there are two copies of
one encoding in the tree (v6 here, v4 inside web3.js). solana.test.ts pins them against each
other across the byte range and across leading zeros, which is a real cross-check rather than a
hope: a wrong id is a status lookup that misses for ever, in silence.
tsx is a runtime dependency because the unpublished packages resolve to their TypeScript
sources. On publish their publishConfig points at dist/, tsx moves to devDependencies, and the
image runs 'node dist/index.js'.
